claim: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR).
source: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by mutations in CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about cystic fibrosis.

claim: The most frequent mutation (F508del-CFTR) results in altered proteostasis, that is, in the misfolding and intracellular degradation of the protein.
source: The most frequent mutation (F508del-CFTR) results in altered proteostasis, that is, in the misfolding and intracellular degradation of the protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the F508del-CFTR mutation.

claim: Targeting multiple components of signalling pathways resulted in potent and specific correction of F508del-CFTR proteostasis.
source: Targeting multiple components of these signalling pathways resulted in potent and specific correction of F508del-CFTR proteostasis and in synergy with pharmacochaperones.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing effects of targeting signalling pathways.

claim: Targeting signalling pathways shows synergy with pharmacochaperones in correcting F508del-CFTR proteostasis.
source: Targeting multiple components of these signalling pathways resulted in potent and specific correction of F508del-CFTR proteostasis and in synergy with pharmacochaperones.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing synergistic effects between pathway inhibitors and VX-809.

claim: CF is the most common lethal genetic disease in Caucasians.
source: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common lethal genetic disease in Caucasians.
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge about cystic fibrosis.

claim: CFTR is a chloride channel localised to the apical membrane of several epithelial cells.
source: It is caused by mutations in the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene that encodes a chloride channel localised to the apical membrane of several epithelial cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR protein function and localization.

claim: Mutations that cause CFTR loss of function impair the transepithelial movement of salts at the cell surface.
source: Mutations that cause CFTR loss of function impair the transepithelial movement of salts at the cell surface, resulting in pleiotropic organ pathology and, in the lungs, in chronic bacterial infections that eventually lead to organ fibrosis and failure (Riordan, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riordan, 2008.

claim: CFTR loss of function results in pleiotropic organ pathology and chronic bacterial infections in the lungs that eventually lead to organ fibrosis and failure.
source: Mutations that cause CFTR loss of function impair the transepithelial movement of salts at the cell surface, resulting in pleiotropic organ pathology and, in the lungs, in chronic bacterial infections that eventually lead to organ fibrosis and failure (Riordan, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riordan, 2008.

claim: The CFTR protein comprises two membrane-spanning domains, two cytosolic nucleotide-binding domains, and a regulatory domain, folded together into a channel.
source: The CFTR protein comprises two membrane-spanning domains, two cytosolic nucleotide-binding domains, and a regulatory domain, folded together into a channel (Riordan, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riordan, 2008.

claim: CFTR folding occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through the sequential action of multiple chaperone complexes.
source: Folding occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through the sequential action of multiple chaperone complexes (Loo et al., 1998; Meacham et al., 1999; Rosser et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Loo et al., 1998; Meacham et al., 1999; Rosser et al., 2008.

claim: After folding in the ER, CFTR is exported out of the ER and glycosylated in the Golgi before arrival at the plasma membrane (PM).
source: and is followed by export out of the ER and glycosylation in the Golgi before arrival at the plasma membrane (PM), where CFTR undergoes several cycles of endocytosis before degradation in the lysosomes (Gentzsch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gentzsch et al., 2004.

claim: At the PM, CFTR undergoes several cycles of endocytosis before degradation in the lysosomes.
source: and is followed by export out of the ER and glycosylation in the Golgi before arrival at the plasma membrane (PM), where CFTR undergoes several cycles of endocytosis before degradation in the lysosomes (Gentzsch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gentzsch et al., 2004.

claim: The F508del-CFTR mutation is present in ~90% of patients with CF.
source: The most frequent mutant, which is present in ~90% of the patients with CF, misses a phenylalanine at position 508 (F508del-CFTR)
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge about the F508del mutation.

claim: F508del-CFTR folds in a kinetically and thermodynamically impaired fashion into a conformation that is recognized as defective by the ER quality control (ERQC) system.
source: and folds in a kinetically and thermodynamically impaired fashion into a conformation that is recognized as defective by the ER quality control (ERQC) system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about F508del-CFTR folding defects.

claim: F508del-CFTR is retained in the ER and targeted for ER-associated degradation (ERAD) by the ubiquitin–proteasome machinery.
source: It is thus retained in the ER and targeted for ER-associated degradation (ERAD) by the ubiquitin–proteasome machinery (Jensen et al., 1995; Ward et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jensen et al., 1995; Ward et al., 1995.

claim: A small fraction of F508del-CFTR may escape degradation in the ER and reach the PM, where it can function as a channel.
source: A small fraction of F508del-CFTR may escape degradation in the ER and reach the PM, where it can function as a channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about F508del-CFTR behavior.

claim: Patients that express even low levels of functional CFTR channel have milder symptoms.
source: This might have therapeutic relevance because patients that express even low levels of functional channel have milder symptoms (Amaral, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amaral, 2005.

claim: At the PM, F508del-CFTR is recognized by the peripheral (or PM-associated) quality control (PQC) system and is rapidly degraded in the lysosomes.
source: However, at the PM, F508del-CFTR is recognized by the peripheral (or PM-associated) quality control (PQC) system and is rapidly degraded in the lysosomes (Okiyoneda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Okiyoneda et al., 2010.

claim: The UPR and HSR operate as homeostatic reactions that enhance the transcription of the cellular folding machinery.
source: The UPR and HSR operate as homeostatic reactions that tend to redress the imbalances between the load of unfolded proteins and the folding capacity of a cell essentially by enhancing the transcription of the cellular folding machinery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about UPR and HSR mechanisms.

claim: Investigators have sought to induce UPR and HSR by pharmacological means to rescue the F508del-CFTR folding/transport defect, with partial success.
source: Investigators have therefore sought to induce these reactions by pharmacological means with the aim to rescue the F508del-CFTR folding/transport defect, with partial success (Roth et al., 2014; Ryno et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roth et al., 2014; Ryno et al., 2013.

claim: Constitutive trafficking along the secretory pathway is potently controlled by signalling networks triggered by both extra- and intracellular stimuli.
source: We and others have previously shown that constitutive trafficking along the secretory pathway is potently controlled by such signalling networks triggered by both extra- and intracellular stimuli (Cancino et al., 2014; Chia et al., 2012; De Matteis et al., 1993; Farhan et al., 2010; Giannotta et al., 2012; Pulvirenti et al., 2008; Simpson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Many successful drugs target multiple molecular pathways simultaneously with limited toxicity.
source: The choice of this strategy over more traditional approaches such as kinome-wide screenings was based on the rationale that since many of the successful drugs target multiple molecular pathways simultaneously (Lu et al., 2012) and with limited toxicity
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2012.

claim: Changes in gene expression are significant components of the MOAs of many drugs.
source: Changes in gene expression are significant components of the MOAs of many drugs (Popescu, 2003; Santagata et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Popescu, 2003; Santagata et al., 2013.

claim: The gene signatures of 13 correctors were obtained using immortalised CF bronchial epithelial (CFBE41o-) cells on an Agilent microarray platform.
source: The gene signatures of 13 correctors were obtained in our laboratories using immortalised CF bronchial epithelial (CFBE41o-) cells (Kunzelmann et al., 1993) on an Agilent microarray platform (CFBE dataset; see Supplementary file 1 and GEO accession number GSE67698 for the expression profiles).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Another 11 signatures were extracted from the MANTRA database based on the Affymetrix platform.
source: Another 11 signatures were extracted from the MANTRA (Mode of action by network analysis, [Iorio et al., 2010]; MANTRA dataset) that were based on the Affymetrix platform.
evidence: This describes data sources used in the study.

claim: The FIT analysis resulted in 219 downregulated and 402 upregulated CORE genes.
source: The FIT analysis of the gene signatures resulted in 219 downregulated and 402 upregulated CORE genes (Supplementary file 3; Figure 1D; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Each CORE gene was shared by 70% of the corrector signatures.
source: Each of these CORE genes were shared by 70% of the corrector signatures.
evidence: This describes the threshold used in the FIT analysis.

claim: The number of CORE genes was threefold higher than that expected on a random basis.
source: The number of CORE genes were threefold higher than that expected on a random basis (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis described in the methods.

claim: There are extensive and statistically significant protein-protein interactions between CORE genes and F508del-CFTR proteostasis-relevant genes.
source: We found extensive and statistically significant (see Materials and methods) protein-protein interactions among the nodes of the union of these two datasets (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is supported by the protein-protein interaction analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 48 folding/degradation and 24 transport-machinery components were found among CORE genes.
source: A search proteostasis components among CORE genes retrieved 48 folding/degradation and 24 transport-machinery components (Supplementary file 5)
evidence: This is based on analysis of the CORE gene pool.

claim: 24 kinases and 6 phosphatases were found among CORE genes.
source: Since our interest was in the identification of signaling networks that regulate proteostasis we also searched for the presence of signalling molecules among CORE genes and found 24 kinases and 6 phosphatases (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the CORE gene pool.

claim: 47 out of the 108 genes tested were found to be active in regulating F508del-CFTR proteostasis.
source: In all, 47 out of the 108 genes tested were found to be active in regulating F508del-CFTR proteostasis (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the screening data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: 32 genes when depleted enhanced the levels of bands B and C by 1.5-fold to more than 10-fold over controls.
source: Of these, 32 genes (when depleted) enhanced the levels of bands B and C by 1.5-fold to more than 10-fold over controls
evidence: This is supported by the screening data.

claim: 15 genes decreased bands B and C by 20–80% of the control levels when depleted.
source: while 15 genes decreased bands B and C by 20–80% of the control levels.
evidence: This is supported by the screening data.

claim: RNF215 depletion increased the levels of band C to over 10-fold the control levels.
source: RNF215 depletion increased the levels of bands C to over 10-fold the control levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The downregulation of anti-correction genes did not change the levels of F508del-CFTR mRNA.
source: It is also to be noted that the downregulation of anti-correction genes did not change the levels of F508del-CFTR mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mitoxantrone increased the levels of both band C and band B of F508del-CFTR.
source: Among these, mitoxantrone was found to potently increase both band C and band B. (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Strong synergistic interactions were observed between various combinations of siRNAs against CKII, CAMKK2, MLK3, and NUP50.
source: Strong synergistic interactions were observed between various combinations of siRNAs against CKII, CAMKK2, MLK3, and NUP50 (a spliceosomal network component) (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: TGF receptors, CDC42, Rac2, and HPK1 are active components upstream of MLK3 in correction.
source: Among the components upstream of MLK3, we found TGF receptors, CDC42, Rac2, and HPK1 to be active in correction (i.e. their depletion induced correction) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the siRNA screening data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MKK7 and JNK2 are active components downstream of MLK3 in the correction pathway.
source: Within the cascade downstream of MLK3, MKK7 (Figure 2A) and further downstream, JNK2 (Figure 3B) were active components
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 3B.

claim: Overexpression of CDC42, MKK7, or JNK2 markedly decreased the levels of both bands B and C of F508del-CFTR.
source: Conversely, when the activity of the MLK3 pathway was enhanced by transfection of the MLK3 activator CDC42 or MKK7 or JNK2 into the CFBE cells, the levels of both bands B and C dropped markedly (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Downregulation of MLK3 did not increase the CFTR mRNA levels.
source: Downregulation of MLK3 did not increase the CFTR mRNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Downregulation of the MLK3 pathway markedly slowed the degradation of band B when measured by CHX chase assay.
source: Downregulation of the MLK3 pathway markedly slowed the degradation of band B when measured by CHX chase assay (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This is supported by the CHX chase data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Overexpression of CDC42, MKK7, or JNK2 increased the rate of degradation of band B twofold.
source: Moreover, for selected genes (MLK3, CAMKK2, RNF215, NUP50 and CD2BP2), the findings from the screening studies were reinforced using additional siRNAs (for instance, five additional siRNAs for MLK3; see Supplementary file 6 for details of the siRNAs used) that showed similar effects on proteostasis of F508del-CFTR (not shown). (3) The coherent effects of the siRNA targeting different genes of signaling pathways supports the functional significance of the effects of each siRNA (see Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). (4) Overexpression of identified hits show an opposite effect on proteostasis to that of the siRNAs (see below Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system itself was not detectably affected by the modulation of the MLK3 pathway activity.
source: Notably, the ubiquitin-proteasome system itself was not detectably affected by the modulation of the MLK3 pathway activity, as judged by the lack of effects on both the proteasome sensor-ZsProsensor-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and the accumulation of poly-ubiquitinated proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the proteasome activity assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Depletion of MLK3 slowed the degradation rate of band C, increasing the t1/2 from ~2 to ~4 hr.
source: Under these conditions, the depletion of MLK3 slowed the degradation rate of band C, increasing the t1/2 from ~2 to ~4 hr (Figure 4E,F)
evidence: This is supported by the PQC assay data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Overexpression of CDC42 enhanced the band C degradation rate.
source: whereas overexpression of CDC42 to activate MLK3 enhanced the band C degradation rate (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is supported by the PQC assay data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Knockdown of JNK2 did not change the degradation kinetics of band C.
source: In contrast, the knockdown of JNK2 (or its overexpression) did not change the degradation kinetics of band C
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from PQC assays.

claim: Treatment with H2O2 at non-toxic concentrations induced a marked drop of the F508del-CFTR levels within 30 min.
source: The effects of H2O2 at non-toxic concentrations were dramatic, with a marked drop of the F508del-CFTR levels within 30 min (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: TNF-α and TGF-β induced rapid 50% decreases in levels of F508del-CFTR.
source: Also TNF-α and TGF-β induced rapid, although less complete (50%) decreases in levels of F508del-CFTR (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The reduction in F508del-CFTR levels induced by H2O2, TNF-α, and TGF-β was completely abolished by MLK3 downregulation.
source: Under these conditions, the reduction in F508del-CFTR levels was completely abolished by MLK3 downregulation (Figure 5A–D)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Three JNK inhibitors (JNKi II, JNKi IX, JNKi XI) led to robust increases in the levels of band B and band C.
source: For JNK, we tested a set of 10 reported JNK inhibitors (JNKi), three of which led to robust increases in the levels of band B and band C (Figure 6A–D; JNKi II, JNKi IX, JNKi XI)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Oxozeaenol markedly increased the bands B and C of F508del-CFTR.
source: Oxozeaenol markedly increased the bands B and C of F508del-CFTR (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The corrective effects of oxozeaenol were not additive with MLK3 knockdown.
source: In line with this notion, the corrective effects of oxozeaenol were not additive with MLK3 knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was potent synergy between MLK3 pathway inhibitors and VX-809.
source: Indeed, when we added both MLK3 pathway inhibitors and VX-809, there was potent synergy between them (Figure 6E,F)
evidence: This is supported by the combination treatment data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: The combination of MLK3 pathway inhibitors and VX-809 resulted in increases in levels of band C that were over 20-fold the basal band C level and fourfold over those obtained with VX-809 alone.
source: Indeed, when we added both MLK3 pathway inhibitors and VX-809, there was potent synergy between them (Figure 6E,F) with increases in levels of band C that were over 20-fold the basal band C level and fourfold over those obtained with VX-809 alone.
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: JNKi II rescued P-gp DY490 and ATP7B mutants.
source: JNKi II rescued some of these mutants (P-gp DY490 and ATP7B mutants), while it had no effects or had 'negative' effects, on others (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: JNKi II had no effect on the proteostasis of endogenous non-mutant proteins including E-cadherin, IGF1R-β and EGFR.
source: We also tested the effect of JNKi II on other endogenous non-mutant proteins (apart from Na+/K+-ATPase that was a reference in many of our treatments) including, E-cadherin, IGF1R-β and EGFR (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) and found no effect on their proteostasis.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The CORE genes were ~3-fold enriched in the signatures of correctors compared to those of other ~200 drugs taken at random from the MANTRA database.
source: The CORE genes were ~3-fold enriched in the signatures of correctors compared to those of other ~200 drugs taken at random from the MANTRA database (not shown).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of gene enrichment.

claim: At least 20% (5 out of 22) of the short-listed drugs from MANTRA were correctors.
source: Thus, at least 20% (5 out of 22) of the short-listed drugs were correctors, while among a large number (>20) of randomly selected drugs none showed correction activity (not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental testing of drugs selected from MANTRA.

claim: The correctors showed a high frequency (two- to threefold more than non-corrector drugs) of upregulation of the potent pro-corrector genes MKK1, MKK3 and FGFBP1.
source: The correctors showed a high frequency (two- to threefold more than non-corrector drugs) of upregulation of the potent pro-corrector genes MKK1, MKK3 and FGFBP1
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression patterns in corrector vs non-corrector drugs.

claim: The non-corrector drugs upregulated more frequently (two- to threefold more than corrector drugs) the anti-corrector genes NF-κB2 and MKK7.
source: while the non-corrector drugs upregulated more frequently (two- to threefold more than corrector drugs) the anti-corrector genes NF-κB2 and MKK7.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression patterns in corrector vs non-corrector drugs.

claim: The physiological role of CORE signalling systems might be to regulate the stringency of the QC and degradation processes.
source: The physiological role of these CORE signalling systems might be to regulate the stringency of the QC and degradation processes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Most of the CORE pathways enhance the efficiency of QC and degradation.
source: Most of the CORE pathways enhance the efficiency of QC and degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that inhibition of these pathways reduces degradation.

claim: The ERBB4 pathway is activated under growth conditions and appears to suppress the QC and degradation processes.
source: The ERBB4 pathway, in contrast, is activated under growth conditions, and appears to have the effect of suppressing the QC and degradation processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and known functions of ERBB4.

claim: Large amounts of ROS are produced by neutrophils in the inflamed lungs of CF patients.
source: For example, large amounts of ROS are produced by neutrophils in the inflamed lungs of CF patients (Witko-Sarsat et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Witko-Sarsat et al., 1995.

claim: Elevated serum VEGF are detected in some CF patients.
source: and elevated serum VEGF are detected in some CF patients (McColley et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McColley et al., 2000.

claim: The simplest interpretation is that inhibition of the MLK3 pathway regulates the folding/degradation switch by impairing the entry of F508del-CFTR into the degradation pathway.
source: The simplest interpretation of the data is therefore that inhibition of the MLK3 pathway regulates this folding/degradation switch by impairing the entry of F508del-CFTR into the degradation pathway and giving the mutant more time to fold and exit the ER.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: HOP co-precipitates much less efficiently with F508del-CFTR in cells treated with JNK inhibitors than in control cells.
source: Some initial insight might come from our observation that the phosphoprotein HOP co-precipitates much less efficiently with F508del-CFTR in cells treated with JNK inhibitors than in control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: HOP serves as a link between HSC70 and HSP90 in the F508del-CFTR folding process.
source: HOP serves as a link between HSC70 and HSP90 in the F508del-CFTR folding process, and its depletion induces rescue of F508del-CFTR (Marozkina et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marozkina et al., 2010.

claim: Over 120 inhibitors against the correction-related kinases identified in this study are currently in clinical trial.
source: For instance, over 120 inhibitors against the correction-related kinases identified in this study (not shown) are currently in clinical trial.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of clinical trials for kinase inhibitors.

claim: JNK has been reported to be hyperactive in the lungs of a mice model of CF.
source: Moreover, JNK has been reported to be hyperactive in the lungs of a mice model of CF (Grassme et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grassme et al., 2014.

claim: p38 MAPK is hyperactive in the lungs of CF patients.
source: as is p38 MAPK (also activated by MLK3) in the lungs of CF patients (Berube et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berube et al., 2010.

claim: The MLK3 pathway inhibitor oxozeaenol has been reported to be effective in correcting the F508del-CFTR proteostasis defect in the primary human bronchial epithelial cells.
source: Also notably, the MLK3 pathway inhibitor oxozeaenol has been reported to be effective in correcting the F508del-CFTR proteostasis defect in the primary human bronchial epithelial cells (Trzcinska-Daneluti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Trzcinska-Daneluti et al., 2012.

claim: TNF-α and TGF-β have been proposed to be genetic modifiers of CF.
source: TNF-α and TGF-β have been proposed to be genetic modifiers of CF (Cutting, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cutting, 2010.

claim: ROS have been reported to be enhanced in CF cells.
source: and ROS have been reported to be enhanced in CF cells (Luciani et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luciani et al., 2010.

claim: The majority of the known drug targets are signalling components.
source: This goal appears realistic, because signalling cascades are eminently druggable (the majority of the known drug targets are signalling components [Imming et al., 2006])
evidence: This is supported by citation to Imming et al., 2006.
